DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
OFFICE OF THE SECRETARY
WASHINGTON, D. C. 20250
May 24, 1971
Mr. Charles J. Orlebeke
Deputy Under Secretary
Department of Housing and Urban Development
Washington, D. C. 20410
Dear Mr. Orlebeke:
We have reviewed the Department of Housing and Urban Development environmental impact statement entitled "Operation Breakthrough" and offer the following comments.
The statement does not deal specifically with ways of handling air pollution, water pollution, soil crosion, visual pollution, fire, noise, and flooding. However, this statement focuses attention on the composite Breakthrough effort rather than on specific sites. We assume the specific environmental factors will be given due consideration on a site-by-site basis.
Rural housing is of no less importance than urban housing. The structural stability and maintenance of housing in both urban and rural areas is tied very closely to locating the houses on land suitable for the intended purpose. This includes sites that are not subject to such physical hazards as flooding, high shrink-swell, and serious crosion hazards.
There is no assurance in this impact statement that some of the land mistakes made in the past will not be repeated again. Many poor quality communities are poor because they were put on poor quality land. This is particularly true when low cost homes were contemplated and subdividers, in their attempt to keep prices down, bought cheap land with many physical hazards and limitations. Then, inability to spend the kinds of monies necessary to overcome these limitations led to low quality communities with such troublesome environmental problems as flooding, waterlogging, inoperative septic tanks, soil erosion, sedimentation, foundation failures, cracking of homes from differential settlement on compressive soils or high shrink-swell soils, disruption of the natural flow of water without adequately providing for accommodating runoff from maximum rainfall events. Inability to accommodate all of these details has led to many distressed communities.
